# Rubber and vulcanisation (`rubber_vulcanisation`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/chemistry.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Chemistry (`chemistry`)
- Core idea: The milky sap of certain tropical trees (Hevea in the Amazon, Castilla in Mesoamerica) dries to an elastic, waterproof gum, but raw rubber turns sticky in heat and brittle in cold. Kneading in a few per cent of sulphur (about 3–8 parts per 100) and heating at 140–160 °C for some hours links the long molecules, giving a tough material that keeps its spring from frost to boiling water. About 30 % sulphur gives hard ebonite. Uses include hoses, seals, tyres, waterproof cloth and electrical insulation.
- Pitfalls:
  - Selling or using uncured rubber goods; they melt in summer, as Goodyear's early ventures showed.
  - Looking for rubber trees in Europe or temperate Asia; Hevea is native to tropical South America; African trees and vines also yield natural rubber.
  - Overheating: it scorches and stinks, and the fumes are noxious.
  - Oil, fat and sunlight slowly destroy natural rubber.
- History: americas: c. 1600 BC – Olmec and later Mesoamerican peoples cure Castilla latex with morning-glory juice for a range of goods; 1839 Goodyear develops sulphur vulcanisation in the United States (US patent 1844); europe: 1736 La Condamine sends samples; 1770 Priestley notes it rubs out pencil; 1823 Macintosh's waterproof cloth; 1843 Hancock's English patent; 1888 Dunlop's pneumatic tyre; east_asia: 1876–1877 – Hevea seeds taken via Kew to Ceylon and Malaya; plantations dominate after 1910
- Read:
  - Dorothy Hosler, Sandra L. Burkett & Michael J. Tarkanian, Prehistoric Polymers: Rubber Processing in Ancient Mesoamerica, Science 284 (1999)
  - Charles Slack, Noble Obsession (2002)
